After it annotates a unit (one kept scaffold, see
[Get started](RiboPilot.html#samples-scaffolds-and-records)), RiboPilot runs a
set of automatic quality checks and
raises a **curation warning** for anything that looks unusual. Warnings guide
your attention in the Annotation Review step. They do not change your data, and a
warning does not always mean something is wrong: it means "please check this".

You see them in three places:

- the **Checks** column of the Assemble and Annotation Review tables (right after
  the ID, or after **Path #** and **Scaffold #** when those show), which sums up
  every check in a few words;
- the **Warnings** column of Annotation Review, which counts the warnings on the
  unit as a whole (marked "unit" in the table below); hover over it for the list;
- the **Curation warnings** panel of a unit's window, which lists the unit's
  warnings and, below them, each feature that has a warning. Click **select** on a
  feature's row to make it the active feature.

# What the warnings mean

| Warning | On | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| `missing_18S`, `missing_5.8S`, `missing_28S` | unit | One of the three rRNA genes was not found. | Expected when the scaffold holds only part of the repeat. Otherwise look at **Read coverage** for a break. |
| `missing_ITS1`, `missing_ITS2` | unit | A spacer was not found between its two genes. | Usually follows a missing gene. If both genes are there, check the boundaries in **Edit active feature boundaries**. |
| `out_of_order` | unit | The features are not in the order 18S, ITS1, 5.8S, ITS2, 28S. | Likely a misassembly; the export marks it `misassembly`. Check the feature map and read coverage before you submit it. |
| `overlap` | unit and feature | A feature overlaps the one before it. | Move the boundary in **Edit active feature boundaries**. The export marks it `misassembly`. |
| `gap` | unit and feature | Bases between two neighboring features that belong to neither. Gaps of 5 bases or fewer are closed when the unit is annotated, so a new unit only gets `gap` for a larger one; after you edit a boundary, any gap is flagged. | Check the boundaries, and extend the gene or spacer if the gap is part of it. |
| `wrong_strand` | unit and feature | A feature lies on the opposite strand from the rest. | Likely a misassembly or a wrong call. Check the feature model. |
| `length` | feature | The feature is shorter or longer than the range for its group (tables below). | Common for the spacers, and often fine. Check that the boundaries look right. |
| `truncated` | feature | Less than 90 percent of the gene's rRNA model was recovered. | Nothing: the export writes the gene as partial. |
| `low_identity` | feature | The gene is less similar to its best reference than the floor for its group (tables below), and the reference covers at least half of the gene. | An assembly error, or a little-studied group. Look at the **Reference alignment**. |
| `contaminant` | unit | The BLAST screen's best hit is from a different phylum than your sample. | Check the unit before you lock it: it may be another organism's rDNA. Lock and the Export window ask about it until you mark it Reviewed. |
| `contaminant_unchecked` | unit | The contamination check could not run: the BLAST screen has no usable hit for the unit, or your sample's lineage is unknown. | If NCBI could not be reached, run the sample again once it can (see [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.html)). If the sample has no taxon, set one in the Taxonomy step. |
| `not_nuclear_rdna` | unit | The BLAST screen's best hit is not a nuclear rDNA record, for example a mitochondrial or bacterial rRNA. | The scaffold may not be nuclear rDNA. Check its features and hits before you keep it. |
| `no_clade_ruleset` | unit | Your sample's group has no ruleset of its own, so the generic animal ranges were used. | Nothing. See [How the checks are tuned per group](#how-the-checks-are-tuned-per-group). |

Two more columns hold checks of their own. **ITSx Warnings** says what stock ITSx, the
tool NCBI runs on rRNA and ITS submissions, finds in the unit, for example
`itsx_chimeric`, `itsx_no_5.8S`, or `itsx_boundary_shift(...)`. **Chimera** holds the
chimera check's level; see [Chimeras](#chimeras-scaffolds-made-of-two-pieces).

The contamination checks need a BLAST screen result. When a unit has none, for
example because NCBI could not be reached, RiboPilot does not skip the check: it
raises `contaminant_unchecked`, and triage flags the scaffold "BLAST screen has not
run".

`low_identity` needs the reference sequences it compares each gene against, which
the run downloads from NCBI (or reuses from your reference folder). When they could
not be downloaded, the identity check is skipped with no warning, so a gene without
`low_identity` has not always been checked.

# The Checks column

The Checks column puts every check on one line, worst first, in a color that
matches the worst finding. On the Assemble table it covers the sample's kept
scaffolds; on the Annotation Review table, one unit. "warnings" means a unit warning from
the table above, the ones the Warnings column counts; "feature flags" means a
warning on one of its features.

| Checks says | Color | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| off target, contaminant, severe chimera, ITSx chimeric | red | Lock and the Export window ask first, until the unit is marked Reviewed. |
| minor chimera, uncertain screen, ITSx, warnings, feature flags | amber | Worth a look; nothing asks. |
| ok | green | The BLAST screen matched your sample's lineage, and nothing is flagged. |
| no reference | grey | Nothing is flagged, but the BLAST screen had no usable match to judge by. |

# What the BLAST screen searches

After a scaffold is assembled, RiboPilot BLASTs it to find out what it matches.
This BLAST screen feeds the Screen column, the contamination warnings above, the
triage rules below, and the chimera check.

By default each scaffold is searched in the **bundled rDNA database** inside the
container: about 600,000 animal nuclear rDNA records from GenBank, plus NCBI's
16S, eukaryote small subunit, and eukaryote large subunit rRNA sets, so that a
bacterial, fungal, or plant scaffold still finds its match. Only a scaffold that
matches nothing there is sent on to NCBI's full nucleotide database (core_nt),
over the internet. Neither search is filtered to nuclear rDNA titles, and a
scaffold the bundled database cannot match goes on to core_nt, so a
mitochondrial or bacterial scaffold is still caught (unless you choose
"Bundled database only").

To change this, open a sample's **BLAST Options** in the Assemble step and pick a
**Search** choice: "Bundled database only" never goes to NCBI, and "NCBI only
(core_nt)" skips the bundled database. The BLAST Options window also names the
version of the bundled database.

The line under the scaffold name in the **BLAST evidence** panel (click a
sample's ID in the Assemble step, "Best match in ...") says which database
gave the scaffold's best match. In Annotation
Review, the **Hit Source** column (in the **BLAST** column group) says which
database named the unit's best rDNA reference: "bundled", "NCBI", or "seed file"
(the assembly's own seed database, which is only a hint).

For a methods section, see [Citing RiboPilot](Citing.html).

# How scaffolds are kept or dropped (auto-triage)

Warnings point at something worth a look; they never remove data. Separately,
once a scaffold has been annotated and screened, RiboPilot proposes keep, drop,
or undecided for the scaffold itself, in the Assemble step. You can override
every call by hand with **K** and **D**, and your own decisions are never
silently overwritten (more on that below).

The proposal rests on two evidence channels that are independent of one
another: **annotation**, from barrnap and ITSx run on the scaffold, and the
**BLAST screen** described above. RiboPilot never drops a scaffold on one
channel's silence: a rule can only drop once both the annotation tools and the
BLAST screen have reported on the scaffold. By default, the only rule that drops
is the one where both channels independently say the scaffold is not nuclear
rDNA. Three other rules can be switched to Drop as well: two fire when
annotation and the BLAST screen *disagree* with each other, and one fires when
the BLAST screen's own consensus disagrees with the sample's identity. Turning
any of them on is a deliberate choice about which evidence you trust more for
your material, not more of the same corroboration; see the table below for
which is which.

RiboPilot checks a scaffold against eight named rules, in this order. The
first rule that matches decides the outcome; if none match, the scaffold is
kept. Four of the eight rules can ever drop a scaffold. The other four only
flag, because their evidence is a missing channel, taxonomic distance alone, or
a possible chimera, none of which is a safe basis for removing a scaffold by
itself. A flagged scaffold stays undecided, and the **Why** column of the
sample's scaffold table gives the reason.

| # | Rule | What it means | Can it drop? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Annotation has not run | Neither annotation tool has reported on this scaffold yet. | No, flag only |
| 2 | BLAST screen has not run | No usable BLAST hit is recorded, so the scaffold cannot be judged. | No, flag only |
| 3 | No annotations, non-rDNA hit | Annotation found no rRNA or ITS feature, and the best GenBank match is not a nuclear rDNA record. | Yes, dropped by default |
| 4 | No annotations but rDNA hit | Annotation found no rRNA or ITS feature, though the best GenBank match is a nuclear rDNA record. | Optional; flagged by default |
| 5 | Has annotations but non-rDNA hit | The scaffold has a feature model, but its best GenBank match is not a nuclear rDNA record. | Optional; flagged by default |
| 6 | GenBank taxonomy disagrees with the sample | The scaffold's BLAST hits agree on a taxon that is not on this sample's lineage. | Optional; flagged by default |
| 7 | Disagrees with sibling scaffolds | This scaffold's top hit disagrees with the majority of this sample's other scaffolds. | No, flag only |
| 8 | Chimeric assembly (severe) | Parts of this scaffold match organisms from different phyla or kingdoms. | No, flag only |

Rule 2 also covers a case that looks different but is judged the same way: a
scaffold whose only GenBank matches are whole-genome or chromosome-level
assemblies. Such a record does not say what the aligned region actually is, so
RiboPilot reports the scaffold as unjudged rather than guessing that it is not
nuclear rDNA.

Rule 6 is a separate check from the rest of the table: it asks whether the
scaffold's BLAST hits agree on a taxon, and whether that taxon sits on your
sample's own lineage. This is the check that catches a fungal, bacterial or
plant contaminant riding along with a metazoan sample. It compares only
against your sample's own lineage, at phylum rank, so it cannot separate two
metazoans in the same phylum: a human on a fish sample passes, because both
are Chordata, while a copepod on that same sample is caught. A `no_reference`
result is a normal state
for an offline project or a sparse clade, not a problem in itself: it means
the screen had nothing usable to compare against, not that something is
wrong. The verdict is also shown as a Screen column in a sample's scaffold table
(click its ID in the Assemble step) and in the Annotation Review table, and an
off-target verdict turns the Checks cell red.

To change what a rule does, tick samples in the Assemble step and press
**Triage**. The Triage window sets each rule to Off, Flag, or Drop (Drop only
where the rule allows it), shows how many scaffolds each rule would decide, and
applies to the ticked samples when you press **Apply**. Switching every rule off
at once makes Apply a no-op: it changes nothing, rather than marking every
remaining scaffold "keep" on the strength of no active checks. The rule
settings live with the project, not with any one run, so the app and the
pipeline never disagree about what a rule is set to do.

Rule 7 deserves a special note: a low-identity hit at a large taxonomic
distance is the normal state for an under-studied group, not proof of
contamination, which is exactly the case RiboPilot exists to serve. For that
reason, disagreement with sibling scaffolds can only ever flag, never drop.

# Chimeras: scaffolds made of two pieces

A chimera is one scaffold joined from two pieces that do not belong together:
rDNA from two organisms (for example a fish and a contaminating mold), or two
different copies of the repeat from one genome.

RiboPilot looks for a chimera in four ways:

- **Gene by gene.** The 18S, 5.8S, and 28S genes each get their own best
  GenBank matches, and these should agree on one lineage.
- **Along the scaffold.** Overlapping 500 bp windows, one every 250 bp, are
  matched against the bundled rDNA database, and neighboring windows that match the
  same class are joined into segments. Two neighboring segments of similar
  length from different classes suggest a join.
- **Gene structure.** The ribotyper tool checks that the 18S and 28S each look
  like one whole gene. ITSx's own chimera call adds a little weight.
- **Reads.** Many reads that stop at the same point, or a lasting step in read
  depth, can mark a join.

Each unit gets one of three levels, shown in the **Chimera** column of the
Annotation Review table and in the **Checks** column:

| Level | What it means | Triage | Export |
|---|---|---|---|
| severe | Two parts match different phyla or kingdoms, each at 90 percent identity or more. | Rule 8 flags the scaffold. | The `submission_risk` column says `chimeric(...)`, and Lock and the Export window ask first until the unit is marked Reviewed. |
| minor | Weaker evidence: a switch between classes, genes that agree only at a high rank, a ribotyper warning, or read evidence alone. | No rule fires. | Listed in the `chimera_warning` column of the summary CSV. It is not a submission risk, and neither Lock nor the Export window asks. |
| clean | Nothing found. | No rule fires. | Nothing. |

In the practice project, CHIM01 is severe: its first part matches ray-finned
fishes and its 28S matches a *Penicillium* mold, and the plot marks the join
near 2,625 bp:

![Chimera check for a real chimera](figures/curation/chimera-severe.png)

RiboPilot already sets aside the usual false alarms. Windows in conserved
stretches of 18S or 28S, where many groups match equally well, are shown as
"unresolved" and do not count. Depth changes inside sequence that repeats
elsewhere on the scaffold, or right at a gene boundary, are ignored, and so are
reads that stop near the ends of the scaffold. A weak signal can still give a
minor call. The first scaffold of SRR33849683, for example, is minor because its
genes agree only at phylum level, though every window that can be placed
matches a ray-finned fish:

![Chimera check for a weaker signal that needs a look](figures/curation/chimera-mild.png)

To judge a flag, open the **Chimera check** panel, and hover over the unit's
badge in the **Chimera** column to read the evidence behind the call. A real
chimera shows a clean switch from one lineage to another at one point, often
with a depth change there too. A switch that sits inside a conserved stretch of
18S or 28S, to a group that is not far from yours, is usually a false alarm. If
in doubt, copy the scaffold with **Copy FASTA** and BLAST each side at NCBI.

# Several scaffolds from one organism: the Variant column

None of the rules above fires on this, and that is deliberate. When a sample
yields more than one scaffold that the BLAST screen calls on target, both
agree with your sample's lineage at phylum level. That rules out many
contaminants but not all: a human on a fish sample is also a chordate. BLAST
each variant's ITS before you lock one. RiboPilot
compares them and tells you which of two situations you are looking at, in a
Variant column in the Assemble step's scaffold table.

An **isomer** means the scaffolds are the same molecule assembled two ways:
their conserved anchors are the same sequence, and they differ only outside
them. Often that is spacer copy number, because the rDNA repeat's intergenic
spacer contains subrepeats and an assembly graph can traverse a different
number of them on different passes. It is not always: when two isomers have the
same total length the difference cannot be copy number, so RiboPilot reports the
measured length difference and lets you see which case you have. The
comparison looks only at the 18S, 5.8S, and 28S genes. Two isomers can still
differ in ITS1 or ITS2, and if they do, the one you lock is the ITS that GenBank
receives, so compare their ITS before you choose.

A **paralog** means the sample genuinely carries several different rDNA copies.
This is real, documented biology in Octocorallia, Scyphozoa and other groups,
not a defect and not a sign that anything went wrong. Here the choice does
matter, because which scaffold you lock is what GenBank receives. The column is
rendered as information rather than as a warning, and export records the fact
without blocking anything: a paralogous scaffold still exports.

Three details worth knowing. The comparison uses only the conserved anchors
(18S, 5.8S and 28S), because the spacers vary in both situations and so cannot
tell them apart. RiboPilot does not annotate the intergenic spacer as a feature,
so any statement about spacer copy number is inferred from the unannotated
remainder rather than measured directly. And two scaffolds are only compared on
the anchors they **both** carry, and only when enough of each one aligns: a
scaffold whose 28S is a short fragment is reported as not comparable rather than
declared identical to a complete one. The measured anchor identity is always
shown, so you can see the number the label came from rather than only the label.

# Your own decisions stick

If you keep or drop a scaffold by hand, that decision is recorded as yours,
and a later automatic re-run will not overwrite it, even if the rules above
would now propose something different. Re-triaging only touches scaffolds it
decided itself, unless you tick **Also re-decide scaffolds I set by hand** in the Triage window.
They also survive assembling the sample again, as long as the scaffold comes
back with the same sequence; a scaffold whose sequence changed starts undecided.

# Depth is shown, not decided

The scaffold table shows each scaffold's median per-position read depth and a
small sparkline of depth along its length, but depth never decides a keep or
drop call. Reads are mapped to one path at a time, and reads that
could sit in more than one place in that path are set aside. So depth dips
where the sequence repeats inside the path, for example over repeats in the
spacer between units, and those dips are expected. The number is worth a look;
it is not sound enough to decide anything on its own.

# How the checks are tuned per group

The expected lengths and identity floors depend on the group of organisms.
RiboPilot ships five rulesets, and picks one from each sample's lineage:

| Ruleset | Used for samples in |
|---|---|
| `actinopterygii` | ray-finned fishes |
| `asteroidea` | sea stars |
| `scyphozoa` | true jellyfish |
| `octocorallia` | octocorals |
| `metazoa_generic` | any other group; the unit gets the `no_clade_ruleset` note |

To use another one, pick it as **Clade ruleset** in the sample's **Curate
Options** (Assemble step). Leaving `metazoa_generic` there lets RiboPilot choose
from the lineage.

Expected lengths, in bases. A `length` warning means a feature fell outside its
range, which is common and often fine for the spacers:

| Feature | Generic animal | Ray-finned fishes | Sea stars, jellyfish, octocorals |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18S | 1600 to 2100 | 1750 to 1950 | 1700 to 1900 |
| 5.8S | 140 to 180 | 140 to 175 | 150 to 170 |
| 28S | 2000 to 6000 | 2500 to 5000 | 2000 to 6000 |
| ITS1 | 120 to 1600 | 150 to 1200 | 120 to 1200 |
| ITS2 | 120 to 1600 | 150 to 1200 | 120 to 1200 |

Identity floors, in percent. Below these a gene gets `low_identity`:

| Gene | Generic animal | Ray-finned fishes | Sea stars, jellyfish, octocorals |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18S | 95 | 97 | 93 |
| 5.8S | 93 | 95 | 90 |
| 28S | 80 | 85 | 78 |

The floors are lower for sea stars, jellyfish, and octocorals because GenBank
holds few close relatives for them. In every ruleset, a gene is `truncated` when
less than 90 percent of its rRNA model was recovered, and identity is judged only
when the reference covers at least half of the gene.

# Adding tuning for a new group

If you work on a group that would benefit from its own length ranges, that can be
added. This is a small change to RiboPilot's settings rather than new analysis
code. If you are comfortable with R you can add it yourself (see `rrna_params()`
in the source), but you are also very welcome to
[open an issue](https://github.com/dmacguigan/RiboPilot/issues) describing your
group, and we can help set it up. In the meantime, the generic animal setting
works for any group; it is just more lenient.
